strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple datasets (ImageNet, LSUN-Bedrooms, LSUN-Churches), quantization configurations (W8A8 through W4A3), and metrics (IS, FID, sFID, Precision, Recall) with consistent improvements, particularly strong at ultra-low bits (467.73% IS improvement for W4A3)
Well-motivated problem addressing practical challenges in diffusion model deployment: activation outliers and non-stationary distributions across timesteps
Clear technical presentation with excellent visualizations (Figures 2, 5-10) showing channel-wise outlier reduction across multiple layers and timesteps, plus visual quality comparisons
Hardware-friendly design using symmetric quantization and integer-only operations with proper extraction of normalization factors, enabling efficient deployment on hardware accelerators
Systematic comparison with relevant recent baselines (EfficientDM, PTQ-D, Q-Diffusion, QuEST) and improved convergence characteristics demonstrated in Figure 4
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is applying Hadamard transformation only to activations (Single) rather than both activations and weights (Double), which is a relatively straightforward engineering choice rather than fundamental algorithmic innovation; Hadamard transformation for quantization already explored in prior work (QuaRot [2], Xi et al. [60])

Hardware efficiency claims lack experimental validation: no actual hardware benchmarks (latency, throughput, power), deployment results, or inference speed comparisons; claims rely solely on theoretical analysis without practical validation

Insufficient explanation of why Single Hadamard works well for diffusion models: non-stationary activation dynamics acknowledged but not deeply analyzed; lack of theoretical understanding connecting Hadamard properties to diffusion-specific challenges; interaction with timestep-dependent quantization factors not explored

Critical and unexplained dependence on weight stability: Section 5.2 states accuracy depends on weight stability, but no mechanism (regularization, initialization strategy) is provided; appears empirical rather than designed, limiting method robustness and applicability

Fairness of experimental comparisons questioned: HQ-DM uses symmetric quantization while EfficientDM uses asymmetric; dramatic W4A3 improvement (467.73%) lacks thorough analysis and no symmetric quantization results provided for EfficientDM under identical conditions

Limited ablation study: only Hadamard matrix order (k ∈ {3,4,5,6}) ablated; missing ablations on LoRA contribution, distillation necessity, quantization scheme comparison, timestep-aware factors; no ablation isolating Single Hadamard's contribution from other components

Incomplete implementation details hindering reproducibility: learning rates for different components, LoRA rank specification, training denoising steps, and other critical details relegated to appendix

Limited evaluation scope: only 256×256 image generation; single architecture (UNet-based LDM); no evaluation on other tasks (text-to-image, video) or diffusion model variants; relatively small models tested (LDM-4, LDM-8)

Missing analysis of ultra-low-bit performance: why does the method excel dramatically at W4A3 compared to W4A4? No investigation of the trade-offs and computational costs during training compared to baselines

Theoretical gaps: mathematical properties of Hadamard are standard; connection between activation non-stationarity in diffusion models and Hadamard effectiveness not rigorously established; why uniform distribution property translates to better quantization in diffusion context lacks depth

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem in diffusion model quantization by targeting activation outliers that hinder low-bit deployment
Single Hadamard Transformation is a sensible technical contribution—supporting integer convolutions and avoiding weight outlier amplification compared to Double Hadamard
Extensive experimental validation across multiple datasets (ImageNet, LSUN), architectures (LDM, DiT), and quantization levels with consistent improvements over EfficientDM
Comprehensive ablation studies (Table 5) clearly demonstrate the independent contribution of each component (LSQ, LoRA, Hadamard transformation)
Strong empirical results, particularly at ultra-low activation bits (W4A4: 12.8% IS improvement; W4A3: >100% improvements across metrics)
Demonstrates comparable training efficiency to EfficientDM (Figure 5c) with negligible computational overhead from Hadamard transformation
Clear presentation with effective visualizations showing outlier reduction (Figures 2, 4) and architectural differences (Figure 3)
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty—primarily applies Single Hadamard (from prior work) to activations only rather than Double Hadamard; combines existing techniques (LoRA, LSQ, Hadamard) without fundamental algorithmic innovation

Extreme improvement claims at W4A3 (467.73% IS improvement) raise questions due to EfficientDM baseline instability (IS=8.74); noisy convergence (Figure 5b) and lack of confidence intervals make results hard to verify

Hardware efficiency claims are overstated: (1) claims 'integer-only computation' but FP32 normalization factors remain; (2) no actual inference latency benchmarks on real hardware provided, only training time

Unfair quantization comparison—HQ-DM uses symmetric quantization (losing one effective bit) while EfficientDM uses asymmetric; improvements despite this handicap are claimed but comparisons should use identical schemes

Weight quantization dependency not addressed—paper acknowledges accuracy depends on weight stability but LoRA only fine-tunes, doesn't fundamentally solve weight outlier problem; no analysis of weight characteristics

Missing critical implementation details harm reproducibility: Hadamard matrix order k selection criterion unclear, specific learning rates not provided, no ablation on block size effects, sensitivity analysis absent

Lacks theoretical understanding of why Single Hadamard specifically suits diffusion models beyond empirical outlier reduction; no rigorous analysis connecting outlier reduction to temporal error accumulation
Statistical rigor concerns: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported; single-run results particularly unreliable for noisy W4A3 regime (Figure 5b)
Incomplete baseline comparisons—related work mentions DMQ [17] and MPQDM [7] but no systematic experimental comparison included
Double Hadamard comparison fairness questionable—convolutional layers regressed to Single Hadamard for comparison, making it somewhat circular to show Single Hadamard superiority
Generalization limited to image generation (conditional and unconditional); unknown effectiveness on other modalities or generation tasks
No analysis of failure cases, practical bit-width limits, timestep-specific behavior, or performance at even lower precisions (W2A2, W1A1)

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing activation outliers in low-bit diffusion quantization with clear empirical evidence of the challenge

Technically sound Single Hadamard Transformation approach that cleverly addresses limitations of prior Double Hadamard methods: incompatibility with integer convolutions and weight outlier amplification

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (ImageNet, LSUN), architectures (LDM, DiT), and bit-widths showing consistent improvements, with particularly strong results at ultra-low bits (W4A3)
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating independent contribution of each component and direct comparison validating the Single vs. Double Hadamard design choice
Practical implementation with hardware-friendly symmetric quantization, comparable training efficiency, and efficient sparse integer matrix representation
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and comprehensive experimental tables supporting all claims
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: framework heavily builds on EfficientDM (LoRA + LSQ), and Hadamard transformation is borrowed from QuaRot and prior work; main contribution is applying transformation to activations only, which is incremental

Insufficient theoretical analysis: outlier reduction mechanism provides intuition but lacks rigorous bounds on quantization error reduction; missing formal analysis of gradient flow during QAT and why this is particularly effective for diffusion models

Incomplete related work comparison: QuaRot and Xi et al. mentioned but not thoroughly compared experimentally; only Double Hadamard compared in Table 6, missing comparisons with other outlier mitigation techniques

Missing implementation details affecting reproducibility: unclear algorithm for choosing k, padding strategy when C_i≠m·2^k, justification for H=I when channels are small, and no code availability mentioned

Extreme improvement claims at W4A3 (467.73% IS) involve severe baseline degradation (8.74 IS) making practical relevance questionable; some metrics marked missing in tables complicating complete evaluation

Limited evaluation scope: only image generation tested despite introduction mentioning speech and text; only LDM and DiT architectures; no failure mode analysis or scenarios where method underperforms
Asymmetric vs. symmetric quantization trade-off acknowledged but not thoroughly evaluated; claims of hardware-friendliness lack actual hardware speedup measurements
Some presentation issues: notation clarity (H vs H_k vs H_raw_k), convolution transformation along width dimension not justified as optimal, Equation 12 uses '≈' without error analysis
